title: Electrical Circuits: Current, Resistance and Power
seo_title: Year 11 Physics: Electrical Circuits Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Charge, current and potential difference; resistance and Ohm's law; series and parallel circuits; electrical power and energy, the kilowatt-hour; e.m.f. and internal resistance; electrical safety. (Senior Secondary Physics, Unit 1: Thermal, nuclear and electrical physics)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Physics worksheets on electric circuits: current, potential difference, Ohm's law, resistivity, series and parallel circuits, power, kWh and internal resistance. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Series: resistances add. Parallel: reciprocals add.
body_html:
How to think about it

Current is the rate of flow of charge (I = Q ÷ t); potential difference is energy per unit charge (V = W ÷ q); resistance R = V ÷ I. In series the current is the same and R = R₁ + R₂; in parallel the voltage is the same and 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.

Power P = VI = I²R = V² ÷ R. Energy bills use kilowatt-hours: E (kWh) = P (kW) × t (h). A real cell has internal resistance: ε = V + Ir.

Example

Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel?

1/R = 1/6 + 1/6

R = 3 Ω

Answer: 3 Ω

Example

A 230 V kettle draws 8.0 A. Power?

P = VI = 230 × 8.0

Answer: 1840 W

Common mistakes

  • Adding parallel resistances like series ones.
  • Connecting a voltmeter in series.
  • Using watts with hours without converting to kilowatts for kWh.

faq.q: Why does adding a resistor in parallel lower the total resistance?
faq.a: It gives the current another path, so more current flows for the same voltage.
The energy used by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour: 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Electricity bills charge per kWh.

items.e: There are more paths for the current.
